title: First Spot a Needle Appears
statement:
You get two strings, haystack and a non-empty needle. Return the index in haystack where needle first appears as a contiguous substring, or -1 if it never does.

Do it without the language's built-in search (indexOf, includes, find, in). The point is to write the matching yourself.

examples.why: "pap" fails on its last letter; the match starts at index 2: p, a, y.
The attempt at 0 matches "aa" and then fails on "a" vs "b". The real match starts at 1, inside that failed attempt. If you resume after the failed letters instead of backing up, you miss it.
All three letters occur, but never in that order next to each other.

constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: The straightforward way tries every start and compares letter by letter. When is that slow?

On text like "aaaa…ab" with a needle like "aaa…ab", each start compares almost the whole needle before failing. After a failure, you already know the letters you just read. Can you avoid rereading them?

Precompute, for every prefix of the needle, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix (the KMP failure table). On a mismatch, fall back to that length instead of restarting, and the haystack pointer never moves backwards.

explain.intuition:
The simple method is fine on normal text, because mismatches usually happen on the first letter or two. It breaks on repetitive input: with a needle of 40 000 as and a b, every start reads 40 000 letters before failing.

Knuth–Morris–Pratt fixes this by never re-reading the haystack. When you have matched j letters of the needle and then hit a mismatch, those j letters are the needle's own prefix. So the next possible match can only line up with a part of that prefix that is also its suffix. A table built from the needle alone, fail[j] = the longest proper prefix of needle[0..j] that is also a suffix of it, tells you how far you can fall back while keeping what you already matched.
steps: Build fail: walk the needle with k = current border length. On a mismatch, set k = fail[k − 1] until it matches or k = 0; on a match, increase k. Store fail[i] = k.
Walk the haystack with i and keep j = letters of the needle currently matched.
If they match, increase j. When j equals the needle length, return i − j + 1.
If the haystack runs out, return −1.
pitfalls: After a mismatch in the simple method, continuing from where the mismatch happened instead of from start + 1. That misses overlapping matches, as in the second example.
In the table, falling back only once instead of looping. A mismatch may need several fallbacks.
Trying starts past haystack.length − needle.length, which reads beyond the end or wastes time.

solutions.title: Try every start
solutions.idea: For each possible start, compare the needle letter by letter and stop at the first mismatch.

solutions.title: Knuth–Morris–Pratt
solutions.idea: A failure table built from the needle says how much of the current match survives a mismatch, so the haystack is read once.

followups: Return every start index, including overlapping ones. What do you do after a full match in KMP?
Search for many needles at once in one pass over the text. Which structure generalises the failure table?
lcTitle: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
